claim: Healthy young participants (N=75) underwent structural and functional imaging prior to and following the training.
source: Healthy young participants (N=75) underwent structural and functional imaging prior to and following the training.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and imaging protocol in the abstract.

claim: There was no evidence for changes to gross hippocampal volume due to the training.
source: Based on pre-registered and exploratory analyses, we did not find any evidence for changes to gross hippocampal or hippocampal subfield volume, cortical brain volume, or microstructural properties of major white matter tracts due to the training.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the null findings for hippocampal volume changes.

claim: There was no evidence for changes to hippocampal subfield volume due to the training.
source: Based on pre-registered and exploratory analyses, we did not find any evidence for changes to gross hippocampal or hippocampal subfield volume, cortical brain volume, or microstructural properties of major white matter tracts due to the training.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the null findings for hippocampal subfield volume changes.

claim: There was no evidence for changes to cortical brain volume due to the training.
source: Based on pre-registered and exploratory analyses, we did not find any evidence for changes to gross hippocampal or hippocampal subfield volume, cortical brain volume, or microstructural properties of major white matter tracts due to the training.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the null findings for cortical brain volume changes.

claim: There was no evidence for changes to microstructural properties of major white matter tracts due to the training.
source: Based on pre-registered and exploratory analyses, we did not find any evidence for changes to gross hippocampal or hippocampal subfield volume, cortical brain volume, or microstructural properties of major white matter tracts due to the training.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the null findings for white matter microstructure changes.

claim: Network-based analyses suggested changes in task-related informational connectivity.
source: In contrast, network-based analyses suggested changes in task-related informational connectivity, which occurred primarily between cortical areas and mostly involved putative cognitive control networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that network analyses revealed changes in informational connectivity.

claim: Changes in task-related informational connectivity occurred primarily between cortical areas.
source: In contrast, network-based analyses suggested changes in task-related informational connectivity, which occurred primarily between cortical areas and mostly involved putative cognitive control networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the anatomical location of connectivity changes.

claim: Changes in task-related informational connectivity mostly involved putative cognitive control networks.
source: In contrast, network-based analyses suggested changes in task-related informational connectivity, which occurred primarily between cortical areas and mostly involved putative cognitive control networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies the networks showing connectivity changes.

claim: Cognitive interventions target more transient configurations in network connectivity rather than more durable structural changes.
source: These results suggest that cognitive interventions target more transient configurations in network connectivity rather than more durable structural changes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this interpretation of the results.

claim: Improving cognitive skills can contribute positively to multiple aspects of daily life, such as education and professional endeavors.
source: Improving cognitive skills can contribute positively to multiple aspects of daily life, such as education and professional endeavors (Edwards et al., 2018; Kraft et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The neural changes underlying cognitive skill acquisition remain an unresolved question in cognitive neuroscience.
source: Yet, the neural changes underlying cognitive skill acquisition remain an unresolved question in cognitive neuroscience, limiting our ability to target interventions designed to improve these skills.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Some past studies have suggested a relationship between cognitive skills and focal gray matter volume.
source: Some past studies have suggested a relationship between cognitive skills and focal gray matter volume (Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004; Draganski et al., 2006; Engvig et al., 2010; Hänggi et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2000; Wenger et al., 2021), although many of these studies have involved comparison of experts with non-experts or specialized populations (e.g. older adults with cognitive decline).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Many studies showing a relationship between cognitive skills and focal gray matter volume have involved comparison of experts with non-experts or specialized populations.
source: Some past studies have suggested a relationship between cognitive skills and focal gray matter volume (Boyke et al., 2008; Draganski et al., 2004; Draganski et al., 2006; Engvig et al., 2010; Hänggi et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2000; Wenger et al., 2021), although many of these studies have involved comparison of experts with non-experts or specialized populations (e.g. older adults with cognitive decline).
evidence: The text explicitly notes this limitation of prior studies.

claim: It remains unclear whether gray matter volume differences underlie the behavioral changes that occur as part of new cognitive skill acquisition in healthy younger adults.
source: Therefore, it remains unclear whether gray matter volume differences underlie the behavioral changes that occur as part of new cognitive skill acquisition and whether the same mechanisms apply to healthy younger adults.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this as an unresolved question.

claim: Other studies have suggested the importance of changes in either the recruitment of specific brain areas or interactions between brain regions that may not result in macroscopic structural changes.
source: Other studies have suggested the importance of changes in either the recruitment of specific brain areas (i.e. functional activation) or interactions between brain regions (i.e. functional connectivity) that may not result in macroscopic structural changes (Braun et al., 2015; Dresler et al., 2017; Kraft et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The hippocampus is thought to be broadly important to memory.
source: Past studies suggest such overlap for a brain region thought to be broadly important to memory, the hippocampus (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Spiers et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: People with better navigation and/or verbal memory skills typically have larger hippocampi.
source: People with better navigation and/or verbal memory skills typically have larger hippocampi (Brunec et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Poppenk et al., 2013), although this finding has not been consistently replicated (Clark et al., 2020; Weisberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature, with a caveat about replication.

claim: The finding that people with better navigation and/or verbal memory skills have larger hippocampi has not been consistently replicated.
source: People with better navigation and/or verbal memory skills typically have larger hippocampi (Brunec et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Poppenk et al., 2013), although this finding has not been consistently replicated (Clark et al., 2020; Weisberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that failed to replicate the finding.

claim: Transfer of newly trained cognitive skills to other cognitive domains is often modest.
source: Alternatively, it might be that learning different cognitive skills targets only partially overlapping or even independent brain networks, which in turn might hint at why transfer of newly trained cognitive skills to other cognitive domains is often modest (Sala and Gobet, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some studies suggest only partial overlap between navigation and verbal memory.
source: For example, some studies suggest only partial overlap between navigation and verbal memory (Ekstrom and Hill, 2023; Fan et al., 2021; Weisberg and Newcombe, 2016), and it is possible that some of the observed differences between experts and non-experts in past studies arose due to partial overlap between verbal memory and navigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Between-participant designs may be underpowered compared to within-participant approaches.
source: One issue with comparing experts and non-experts is that they involve between-participant designs, which may be underpowered compared to within-participant approaches (Marek et al., 2022) and may introduce other uncontrolled variables.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Successful cognitive interventions suggest that targeted within-participant cognitive training, even for as little as 1–2 weeks, can result in improvements to specific cognitive functions, including changes in focal gray matter.
source: Successful cognitive interventions suggest that targeted within-participant cognitive training, even for as little as 1–2 weeks, can result in improvements to specific cognitive functions, including changes in focal gray matter (Chavan et al., 2015; Colom et al., 2016; Draganski et al., 2004; Driemeyer et al., 2008; Lövdén et al., 2012; Miró-Padilla et al., 2021); but see Ganesan et al., 2024.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature, with a caveat about a contradictory study.

claim: Interventions may generalize to areas not explicitly trained but closely related to the training (termed 'near transfer').
source: In some instances, interventions may even generalize to areas not explicitly trained but closely related to the training (termed 'near transfer'; Jaeggi et al., 2014; Judd and Klingberg, 2021; Karbach and Verhaeghen, 2014; Schmiedek et al., 2010; Schweizer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, each of which consisted of 10 training sessions.
source: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, each of which consisted of 10 training sessions, separated by at least one day over the course of approximately 4–8 weeks (4.12±1.87 weeks).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the experimental design.

claim: Training sessions were separated by at least one day over the course of approximately 4–8 weeks.
source: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, each of which consisted of 10 training sessions, separated by at least one day over the course of approximately 4–8 weeks (4.12±1.87 weeks).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the timing of training sessions.

claim: Each training session lasted 2 hr.
source: Each training session lasted 2 hr.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the duration of training sessions.

claim: A total of 29 participants were recruited for the navigation training condition, with 27 successfully completing 10 sessions.
source: In the navigation training condition, we recruited a total of 29 participants, with 27 successfully completing 10 sessions of navigation training in a large city-scale virtual environment ('Virtual Arida', Figure 1b left).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports recruitment and completion numbers.

claim: Participants in the navigation training condition navigated in a large city-scale virtual environment called 'Virtual Arida'.
source: In the navigation training condition, we recruited a total of 29 participants, with 27 successfully completing 10 sessions of navigation training in a large city-scale virtual environment ('Virtual Arida', Figure 1b left).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the training environment.

claim: Participants improved over the course of navigation training, showing higher error initially for subsection A compared to subsection B, which was significantly reduced for subsection C.
source: Participants improved over the course of the training, showing higher error initially for subsection A (M=79.09, SD = 33.22) compared to subsection B (M=65.52, SD = 26.89), which was significantly reduced for subsection C (M=47.44, SD = 31.22).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 1b shows the data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of subsection on navigation training performance (F(2, 42)=13.46, p<0.001, η2=0.39).
source: We observed a significant main effect of subsection F(2, 42)=13.46, p<0.001, η2=0.39; removing sex and site from the model did not change the effect (Appendix 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the statistical test result.

claim: A total of 32 participants were recruited for the verbal memory condition, with 27 successfully completing 10 sessions of training.
source: In the verbal memory condition, we recruited a total of 32 participants, with 27 successfully completing 10 sessions of training.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports recruitment and completion numbers.

claim: Participants in the verbal memory condition were trained on a time-based method of loci ('temporal method of loci') to improve their verbal memory.
source: They were trained on a time-based method of loci ('temporal method of loci') to improve their verbal memory (Bouffard et al., 2018).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the training method with a citation.

claim: The slopes of the regression lines for the first 5 days and the last 5 days of verbal memory training were both significantly greater than zero.
source: The slopes of the regression lines for the first 5 days and the last 5 days were calculated separately (Figure 1a right), as the training paradigm differed between these two phases (see Methods). Both slopes were significantly greater than zero, indicating a significant improvement in memory performance over the training period: first 5 days, t(26) = 16.971, p<0.001; last 5 days, t(26) = 23.579, p<0.001.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 1a shows the data.

claim: A total of 22 participants were recruited for the active control condition, with 21 successfully completing 10 sessions of watching videos.
source: In the active control condition, we recruited a total of 22 participants, with 21 successfully completing 10 sessions of watching videos.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports recruitment and completion numbers.

claim: The percentage of correct responses on video control questions each day was significantly higher than a 50% guess rate.
source: We did not expect to find a training effect (i.e. improved performance on the questions over sessions), but did find that the percentage of correct responses each day was significantly higher than a 50% guess rate (Figure 1c right, ts(20) > 8.28, ps <0.001, mean = 88.58%, SD = 5.82%), indicating that participants were engaged with the video content.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 1c shows the data.

claim: All three groups demonstrated an increase in learning rate from pre to post on the Navigation Transfer task.
source: Paired-sample t-tests indicated that all three groups demonstrated an increase in learning rate from pre to post, with the Navigation group showing the largest effect (Figure 2a; Navigation: t(26) = 4.43, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.32; Verbal Memory: t(26) = 2.31, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.596; Video Control: t(18) = 3.97, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.20).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 2a shows the data.

claim: The Navigation group showed the largest effect size for learning rate improvement on the Navigation Transfer task.
source: Paired-sample t-tests indicated that all three groups demonstrated an increase in learning rate from pre to post, with the Navigation group showing the largest effect (Figure 2a; Navigation: t(26) = 4.43, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.32; Verbal Memory: t(26) = 2.31, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.596; Video Control: t(18) = 3.97, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.20).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports effect sizes, and Figure 2a shows the data.

claim: Only the Verbal Memory group showed a significant increase in learning rate from pre-test to post-test on the Verbal Memory Transfer task.
source: Paired-sample t-tests indicated that only the Verbal Memory group showed a significant increase in learning rate from pre-test to post-test (Figure 2b; Verbal Memory: t(25) = 3.32, p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.608; Navigation: t(26) = 0.488, p=0.63, Cohen's d=0.113; Video Control: t(20) = –0.55, p=0.588, Cohen's d=0.164).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 2b shows the data.

claim: There was no significant main effect of session on total hippocampal volume (F(1, 71)=0.199, p=0.657, η2=0.0002).
source: The analysis revealed no significant main effect of session (F(1, 71)=0.199, p=0.657, η2=0.0002, BF10=0.151, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of session), no significant main effect of condition (F(2, 71)=0.113, p=0.893, η2=0.003, BF10=0.241, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of condition), and no significant interaction between session and condition (F(2, 71)=1.224, p=0.300, η2=0.003, BF10=0.054, strong evidence against the inclusion of the interaction effect).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical test results.

claim: There was no significant main effect of condition on total hippocampal volume (F(2, 71)=0.113, p=0.893, η2=0.003).
source: The analysis revealed no significant main effect of session (F(1, 71)=0.199, p=0.657, η2=0.0002, BF10=0.151, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of session), no significant main effect of condition (F(2, 71)=0.113, p=0.893, η2=0.003, BF10=0.241, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of condition), and no significant interaction between session and condition (F(2, 71)=1.224, p=0.300, η2=0.003, BF10=0.054, strong evidence against the inclusion of the interaction effect).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical test results.

claim: There was no significant interaction between session and condition on total hippocampal volume (F(2, 71)=1.224, p=0.300, η2=0.003).
source: The analysis revealed no significant main effect of session (F(1, 71)=0.199, p=0.657, η2=0.0002, BF10=0.151, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of session), no significant main effect of condition (F(2, 71)=0.113, p=0.893, η2=0.003, BF10=0.241, moderate evidence against the inclusion of the main effect of condition), and no significant interaction between session and condition (F(2, 71)=1.224, p=0.300, η2=0.003, BF10=0.054, strong evidence against the inclusion of the interaction effect).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical test results.

claim: None of the three training groups exhibited significant changes in total hippocampal volume from pre to post-test.
source: Paired t-tests further confirmed that none of the three training groups exhibited significant changes in total hippocampal volume from pre to post-test (Figure 3b, ps >0.265).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 3b shows the data.

claim: None of the three training groups exhibited significant changes from pre to post-test in any of the six MTL subregions (CA1, CA23DG, SUB, ERC, PRC, PHC).
source: Paired-sample t-tests confirmed that none of the three training groups exhibited significant changes from pre to post-test in any of the six MTL subregions (Figure 3a, ps >0.588, FDR corrected).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 3a shows the data.

claim: Training did not result in any measurable cortical volumetric changes.
source: Paired-sample t-tests revealed that none of the ROIs exhibited significant volume changes from pre- to post-test in any of the three groups (ps >0.697, FDR-corrected). These findings suggest that training did not result in any measurable cortical volumetric changes.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings and interpretation.

claim: No DWI measures changed as a result of the training.
source: Paired-sample t-tests confirmed that none of the three training groups exhibited significant changes from pre- to post-test in any of the seven ROIs (ps >0.083, FDR corrected). These findings remained nonsignificant after controlling for sex and site as covariates (ps >0.063, FDR corrected). Analyses involving WM-FW and GM regions (GM-fwcFA and GM-FW) were also not significant (see Appendix 1). These findings suggest that no DWI measures changed as a result of the training.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings and interpretation.

claim: Neither navigation nor verbal memory training for 20 hr across 10 sessions was sufficient to induce changes in macroscopic hippocampal volume or microstructure of relevant gray matter regions and white matter tracts.
source: Together, these findings suggest that neither navigation nor verbal memory training for 20 hr across 10 sessions was sufficient to induce changes in macroscopic hippocampal volume or microstructure of relevant gray matter regions and white matter tracts.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this conclusion based on the data.

claim: In the Verbal Memory group, the changes in learning rate on the Verbal Memory Transfer task correlated with total hippocampal volume when accounting for sex and site as covariates (r(23) = 0.605, p=0.006, FDR corrected).
source: For the Verbal Memory Transfer task, the changes in learning rate did not correlate with hippocampal volume (r(23) = 0.367, p=0.071). When accounting for sex and site as covariates, however, we found a significant positive correlation (r(23) = 0.605, p=0.006, FDR corrected).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the correlation analysis, and Figure 3d shows the data.

claim: Only the CA23DG subfield showed a positive correlation with the change in learning rate from pre- to post-test in the Verbal Memory Group (r(23) = 0.532, p=0.036, FDR corrected).
source: We further examined the correlation between learning rate and hippocampal subfield volumes after correcting for multiple comparisons (see Methods), specifically focusing on CA1 and CA23DG. Only the CA23DG subfield showed a positive correlation with the change in learning rate from pre- to post-test in the Verbal Memory Group (r(23) = 0.532, p=0.036, FDR corrected, Figure 3c), and this correlation persisted after controlling for sex and site as covariates (r(23) = 0.493, p=0.017).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports the correlation analysis, and Figure 3c shows the data.

claim: Individuals in the Verbal Memory group with larger CA23DG volumes exhibited greater improvement in verbal memory performance from pre- to post-test.
source: These findings suggested that individuals in the Verbal Memory group with larger CA23DG volumes exhibited greater improvement in verbal memory performance from pre- to post-test.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: For the Verbal Memory group, enhanced informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test was observed between the left precuneus and left angular gyrus (t=3.94, p<0.05).
source: For the Verbal Memory group, we observed significantly increased informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test (i.e. post >pre), relative to the combined Navigation and Video Control groups (Figure 4). Specifically, we found enhanced connectivity between the left precuneus and left angular gyrus (t=3.94, p<0.05), the right lateral occipital cortex (LOC) and left intracalcarine (visual) cortex (t=3.63, p<0.05), and the right LOC and left superior parietal lobule (SPL) (t=4.16, p<0.05).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 4 shows the connectivity changes.

claim: For the Navigation group, significantly decreased informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test was observed between the left paracingulate gyrus and right middle frontal gyrus (t=3.80, p<0.05).
source: Conversely, for the Navigation group compared to the combined Verbal Memory and Video Control groups, we observed significantly decreased informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test (i.e. post <pre). Specifically, reduced connectivity was observed between the left paracingulate gyrus and right middle frontal gyrus (MFG) (t=3.80, p<0.05), left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and right supramarginal gyrus (SMG) (t=5.14, p<0.05), left frontal pole and right MFG (t=3.85, p<0.05), left dorsal LOC and right ventral LOC (t=3.7, p<0.05) and right MFG and left MFG (t=3.79, p<0.05).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 4 shows the connectivity changes.

claim: No significant changes in task-related informational connectivity to the hippocampus survived after multiple comparisons correction for either navigation or verbal memory training during encoding.
source: No significant changes in task-related informational connectivity to the hippocampus survived after multiple comparisons correction for either navigation or verbal memory training.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this null finding.

claim: In the Verbal Memory group, significantly decreased informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test during retrieval was observed between the right inferior frontal gyrus and right frontal pole (t=4.01, p<0.05).
source: In the Verbal Memory group, we observed significantly decreased informational connectivity in post-test compared to pre-test (i.e. post <pre) relative to the combined Navigation and Video Control groups. These reductions were identified between the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and right frontal pole (t=4.01, p<0.05), left frontal pole and right SFG (t=4.48, p<0.05), right medial frontal gyrus and right posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (t=4.42, p<0.05), right ventral LOC and left temporo-occipital fusiform cortex (TOFC) (t=4.30, p<0.05), and right lingual gyrus and left SPL (t=3.82, p<0.05).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 5 shows the connectivity changes.

claim: In the Navigation group during retrieval, significantly increased informational connectivity at post-test compared to pre-test was found between the right occipital pole and dorsal LOC (t=4.27, p<0.05).
source: In the Navigation group during retrieval, we found significantly increased informational connectivity in the post-test compared to the pre-test (i.e. post >pre) relative to the combined Verbal Memory and Video Control groups. These increases were found between the right occipital pole and dorsal LOC (t=4.27, p<0.05), and the right SPL and right angular gyrus (AG) (t=4.09, p<0.05).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 5 shows the connectivity changes.

claim: No significant changes in task-related informational connectivity during source retrieval were present to the hippocampus when controlling for multiple comparisons.
source: Again, no significant changes in task-related informational connectivity during source retrieval were present to the hippocampus when controlling for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports this null finding.

claim: A greater distance between spatial and temporal patterns in the left SFG network connectivity during source retrieval was found in the Verbal Memory group at post-test compared to pre-test (t(23) = –4.275, p=0.043, FDR corrected).
source: While no significant changes in pattern distance were observed during the encoding stage for any of the three conditions, a greater distance between spatial and temporal patterns in the left SFG network connectivity during source retrieval was found in the Verbal Memory group at post-test compared to pre-test (t(23) = –4.275, p=0.043, FDR corrected; Figure 6b).
evidence: The Results section explicitly reports statistical findings, and Figure 6 shows the data.

claim: Structural changes in gray and white matter are relatively insensitive to cognitive intervention but are instead reflected in more transient changes to network-based connectivity patterns.
source: From a basic research perspective, our results suggest that structural changes in gray and white matter are relatively insensitive to cognitive intervention but are instead reflected in more transient changes to network-based connectivity patterns.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation of the results.

claim: Both training regimens were effective: participants in the Verbal Memory group were able to learn longer word lists, while participants in the Navigation group were able to reduce the length of their paths and required fewer trials to learn landmarks in new subsections of the environment.
source: Both training regimens were effective: participants in the Verbal Memory group were able to learn longer word lists, while participants in the Navigation group were able to reduce the length of their paths and required fewer trials to learn landmarks in new subsections of the environment.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the training effectiveness.

claim: Baseline hippocampal volume may enable more receptiveness to training.
source: These findings, though exploratory, suggest that baseline hippocampal volume may enable more receptiveness to training, aligning with concepts like neural reserve (Stern, 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation with a citation to the neural reserve concept.

claim: The navigation training partially mimics the training undertaken by London taxi drivers, who first learn individual subsections of an environment before connecting these subsections to one another.
source: Our navigation training is particularly notable in that it partially mimics the training undertaken by London taxi drivers, who first learn individual subsections of an environment before connecting these subsections to one another.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes the similarity to London taxi driver training.

claim: The typical participant showed an improvement from about 25–30 words freely recalled on day 1 to 60–65 words after only five days of verbal memory training.
source: Using this training, we were able to dramatically increase the number of freely recalled words of the average participant, with the typical participant showing an improvement from about 25–30 words freely recalled (repeated) words on day 1 to 60–65 words after only five days of training.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly reports the magnitude of improvement.

claim: Neither the Navigation nor the Verbal Memory group showed macroscopic neural structural differences in the hippocampus.
source: Despite the efficacy of the training, neither the Navigation nor the Verbal Memory group showed macroscopic neural structural differences in the hippocampus, which has been linked to verbal memory and/or navigation function in past studies (Brunec et al., 2018; Burgess et al., 2002; Maguire et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding with citations to prior literature.

claim: These results supply causal evidence supporting the notion that hippocampal structural changes may not impart superior navigation or verbal memory skills.
source: These results supply causal evidence supporting the notion that hippocampal structural changes may not impart superior navigation or verbal memory skills.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation of the results.

claim: London taxi drivers who undergo extensive training to learn the city of London show increased hippocampal volume from pre- to post-training compared to taxi drivers who fail to complete the training.
source: For example, London taxi drivers who undergo extensive training to learn the city of London show increased hippocampal volume from pre- to post-training compared to taxi drivers who fail to complete the training (Maguire et al., 2000).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior literature to contrast with the current findings.

claim: Older adults who undergo an exercise-only training or a navigation + exercise training show reduced hippocampal atrophy compared to a no-contact control.
source: Older adults who undergo an exercise-only training or a navigation + exercise training show reduced hippocampal atrophy (i.e., less volume loss) compared to a no-contact control (Lövdén et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior literature to contrast with the current findings.

claim: In healthy younger adults, there were no observed structural changes to hippocampal gray or white matter tracts, nor were there any significant structural changes to other brain regions.
source: Here, in healthy younger adults, who nevertheless showed robust individual differences in navigation and verbal memory and showed strong evidence of improvement across both types of training, there were no observed structural changes to hippocampal gray or white matter tracts, nor were there any significant structural changes to other brain regions.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the structural findings.

claim: Informational connectivity analyses on fMRI data from a spatial and temporal source memory task revealed unique network reconfiguration signatures as a result of navigation and verbal memory training.
source: In exploratory analyses, informational connectivity analyses on fMRI data from a spatial and temporal source memory task revealed unique network reconfiguration signatures as a result of navigation and verbal memory training.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the functional connectivity findings.

claim: During encoding, increases in connectivity due to the verbal memory training were observed primarily in the frontal and occipital lobes.
source: During encoding, we observed increases in connectivity due to the verbal memory training primarily in the frontal and occipital lobes.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the encoding connectivity findings.

claim: During encoding, decreases in informational connectivity were observed in some of the same areas as a result of navigation training.
source: Conversely, we observed decreases in informational connectivity in some of these same areas as a result of navigation training.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the encoding connectivity findings.

claim: During retrieval, increases in informational connectivity were observed during navigation and decreases during verbal memory training.
source: We observed somewhat of the opposite pattern during retrieval: increases in informational connectivity during navigation and decreases during verbal memory training.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly summarizes the retrieval connectivity findings.

claim: Many connectivity changes were in areas within the frontal cortex, with some longer-range changes to parietal, parahippocampal, and occipital cortex.
source: Again, many of these connectivity changes were areas within the frontal cortex, with some longer-range changes to parietal, parahippocampal, and occipital cortex.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes the anatomical distribution of connectivity changes.

claim: The networks most malleable during acquisition of complex cognitive skills largely involve areas related to cognitive control.
source: Our results suggest that the networks most malleable during acquisition of complex cognitive skills largely involve areas related to cognitive control, with one possibility being that such changes allow modulation of existing networks that include the medial temporal lobe (Schedlbauer and Ekstrom, 2019).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation with a citation.

claim: Navigation and verbal memory training resulted in differential changes within frontal-parietal networks, suggesting that such cognitive skills involve at least partially dissociable changes.
source: At the same time, navigation and verbal memory training resulted in differential changes within these frontal-parietal networks, suggesting that such cognitive skills involve at least partially dissociable changes.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation of the results.

claim: Functional changes that reflect training effects could potentially become solidified through long-term maintenance or the development of domain-specific expertise.
source: In this scenario, functional changes that reflect training effects could potentially become solidified through long-term maintenance or the development of domain-specific expertise.
